subtopic: MR. DOUGLAS (NANAIMO-COWICHAN-THE ISLANDS) - STATEMENTS BY MINISTERS RESPECTING MEMORANDUM ON HIRING OF FRANCOPHONES
MR. DOUGLAS (NANAIMO-COWICHAN-THE ISLANDS) - STATEMENTS BY MINISTERS RESPECTING MEMORANDUM ON HIRING OF FRANCOPHONES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting the rights of all members of the House. I refer to the conflicting and misleading statements which have been made by various members of the cabinet with respect to the memorandum issued by the Public Service Commission concerning the hiring of Francophones. I contend that these misleading statements constitute a contempt of Parliament. If Your Honour agrees that I have a prima facie case of privilege, I would ask leave to introduce a motion for the consideration of the House.
On January 26 the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) tabled the memorandum issued by the Public Service Commission. At page 2752 of Hansard for January 26 the minister described that memorandum in the following terms:
This is in the nature of what I may describe generally as a feasibility study.
I will not take the time of the House to quote the many instances in which the minister and the then Acting Prime Minister said this was not a program but a feasibility study. The fact is that a reading of the memorandum gives an entirely different view of the matter. The opening paragraph of the memorandum reads as follows:
This letter is further to a recent, brief telephone survey of departmental requirements for post-secondary graduates if special funds were made available for 1971. The basis of the survey was a request as to how many additional Francophone graduates you could gainfully employ should the salary costs be covered from funds outside your budgeted programs.
The second paragraph goes on to state:
We are now in a position to clarify some of the aspects of the program. The following factors (although not in order of priority) will be considered.
Then follow 11 factors. The closing two paragraphs state:
In order to avoid any misunderstanding and help speed up the implementation of the program, it is proposed to hold a preliminary meeting on Tuesday, January 12, 1971, at 2:30 p.m. in Place de Ville, Tower "A", 14th floor, room 1430.
It is hoped you will be able to attend and if possible give some thinking as to the practical application of this program, as it applies to your department, before the meeting.
At the foot it says:
N.B.: This information is confidential and no official announcement will be made.
I contend in the first place that this is a program which was under consideration. The minister denied any knowledge of the memorandum. I accept his word that he had not seen it. But it was a program which was under consideration by the various departments.
The second point I want to draw to the attention of the House is that we received misleading and evasive replies as to who was responsible for authorizing the study of this program and who had indicated that $2 million would be available for its implementation. As reported on page 2752 of Hansard for January 26, the President of the Treasury Board said:
I might say that this memorandum outlining a procedure for increasing the proportion of Francophones in the Public Service is not an approved program. It will not be a program approved by the government until it has been submitted to the Treasury Board.
Yet the Treasury Board, as members of the cabinet, had already played a part in authorizing a sum of money for this program.
As reported on page 2753 of Hansard for January 26, I directed the following question to the President of the Treasury Board:
May I ask whether the Public Service Commission or whoever was responsible for formulating this memorandum had authority to say that $2 million would be made available for the purposes stated in the memorandum without the President of the Treasury Board having given his prior consent?
That was a straight question. All the minister had to say was that the government had authorized the expenditure of $2 million and that a program was being prepared. But the minister's reply was:
As I indicated to the Leader of the Opposition, this memorandum is couched, at least in the opening phrases, in the conditional tense, as it should be. Perhaps there is a greater element of certainty in subsequent paragraphs which I do not think is warranted inasmuch as there is no approved program.
As reported on page 2754 of Hansard for January 26, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond asked the President of the Treasury Board to tell the House who, outside the Treasury Board, had the authority to authorize the $2 million. The Minister's reply was as follows:
It is only the Parliament of Canada that can authorize the $2 million.
The fact is, of course, that yesterday the Prime Minister told us that cabinet had already authorized the expenditure of $2 million.
As reported on the same page of Hansard, the President of the Treasury Board said:
There is no program and there will not be a program until such time as formal approval has been given to a proposal. This is a step in the gestation of a proposal, and until it becomes approved it is not a program.

February 3, 1971
Recruitment of Francophones
I should like to draw attention to one other quotation, Mr. Speaker. It is the question which I directed to the Acting Prime Minister on January 28, as reported at page 2843 of Hansard.
Does the Public Service Commission have the authority to commit the government to an additional $2 million annually over and above the regular appropriations, and does it have the authority to set aside the merit system on its own initiative?
The reply of the Acting Prime Minister is clear. He said:
As I said in the House the other day, there has been no money appropriated by Parliament yet for the next year, and before any money would be expended for this purpose not only would the Treasury Board have to approve it, not only would the government have to approve it, but Parliament would have to approve it. No money has been appropriated for this purpose yet.
The government may take refuge in the statement that money had not yet been appropriated, hut the fact is that the expenditure of the money had been authorized. I also refer to the press release that the President of the Treasury Board issued on January 25:
Treasury Board President, Honourable C. M. Drury, stated today that recent press stories purporting to reveal a secret government fund of $2 million for special hiring of Francophones for the Public Service have been seriously misleading.
Then the last paragraph reads:
So far as the $2 million is concerned this has not been allocated to any specific program.
Then I ask the House to look at the statements which were made yesterday, February 2. As reported at page 2982 of Hansard I asked the Prime Minister:
[DOT]-I want to ask the Prime Minister if he knows who did authorize the issuance of this memorandum and, if he did not, would he undertake to find out?

subtopic: MR. DOUGLAS (NANAIMO-COWICHAN-THE ISLANDS) - STATEMENTS BY MINISTERS RESPECTING MEMORANDUM ON HIRING OF FRANCOPHONES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the memorandum was issued pursuant to a decision of cabinet last November.
So it is perfectly clear that the statements made by various ministers disclaiming any knowledge of a proposed plan were just not in accordance with the facts, that last November the proposal had been agreed upon and the Public Service Commission was acting under instructions from the cabinet to prepare such a plan.
As reported at page 2983 of yesterday's Hansard, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) the Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, last November the cabinet authorized the expenditure of an additional $2 million if a feasible plan could be found.
I submit that for an entire week we sought to ascertain from the government who had authorized the plan which was under formulation and we were given evasive and misleading answers. We endeavoured to find out who had indicated to the Public Service Commission that $2 million would be available this year and in subsequent years for the implementation of a program which would be prepared and finally approved, and again we were given misleading and evasive answers. The fact is, of course, that the cabinet had already authorized the preparation

of such a plan and had also authorized the expenditure of this amount of money when the plan was completed.
I want to make it perfectly clear the question of the hiring of Francophones is not at issue at this time.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just taken his seat has sought to have a ruling of the Chair made that his motion raises a prima facie case of privilege.
It is clear, and it has been so established, that the function of the Chair at this point is to determine whether the allegations by the hon. member constitute a prima facie case of privilege. If that were determined by Your Honour, it would then be up to the House to decide whether in fact such privilege existed.
The hon. member has based his question of privilege on what he terms are misleading and evasive replies made by ministers of the government. He has also based his question of privilege on the suggestion that contradictory statements have been made by ministers of the government. I suggest that never in the history of this House has a question of privilege been found to be valid on the basis of conflicting statements made by ministers or any other members. I do not admit for a moment that such conflicting statements have been made, but, indeed, if they were made they do not constitute a question of

privilege in any sense at all. A dispute over facts does not raise a question of privilege; it is a question of debate.
If the leader of the New Democratic Party is asserting that ministers have made conflicting statements or have made evasive replies, this is a dispute over what has happened and he can engage the ministers in debate on an appropriate occasion.
The hon. member went further and said that these ministers had attempted to deceive the House in this case. The hon. member knows as well as I that if he is making the clear statement that ministers of this government have deliberately deceived the House he has one course of action to follow. It is not uncertain as to what he ought to do. If he believes that ministers have deliberately deceived the House-that is, of course, a question of privilege, but he has not said that yet-then he has raised a question of privilege and he ought to follow the time-honoured practice of the House. That practice was decided most recently in 1959 when His Honour, Mr. Speaker Michener, made a ruling that still stands as the ruling affecting privilege in the House, and which was subsequently confirmed by the membership of the House in the vote on that occasion.
It was a very important debate, Mr. Speaker. On that occasion the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), the former Minister of Justice, the Hon. Davie Fulton and others who are in opposition at this time expressed themselves as to what the correct procedure is if a question of privilege is raised affecting the conduct of any member of the House of Commons.
Presumably the leader of the New Democratic Party is asserting to the House that ministers have deliberately misled the House. He is asking for an examination of their conduct by a committee of the House. On that occasion Mr. Fulton, speaking in the debate, made this comment:
In every case, therefore, where a member has really felt that the conduct of any other member of the House of Commons should be examined-
This is what is implied in this motion.
-that member has followed the correct and honourable course of making specific charges so the member concerned will know what it is he has to meet.
In the same debate the right hon. member for Prince Albert insisted upon the necessity of making specific charges. He quoted a statement that had been made by Mr. Mackenzie King when early in the 1940's a member of the House of Commons had made a comment to the effect that the government had produced three new millionaires since the declaration of war. On that occasion Mr. Mackenzie King said:
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member should be obliged either to withdraw the statement completely or else to convert it into a specific charge to be investigated in the usual manner, and the consequences of the investigation also to be followed up in the usual manner.
I could, of course, refer to the judgment of Mr. Speaker Michener. We know that when the conduct of a member on either side of the House is impugned-and Your

speechtext:
Order, please. I have to interrupt the minister and perhaps allow him to conclude his statement in a moment, but it does appear to me that at this point we are embarking on a wrong course. My interpretation of the practice we have followed over the years is that the Chair has allowed a member whose conduct may have been impugned in a statement accompanying a question of privilege to indicate what in his view the facts are and perhaps to rectify the situation as it exists in his own mind. It has not been the practice to debate the procedural point at all.
I am not in disagreement basically with any of the procedural points made by the President of the Privy Council. Indeed, I suspect all hon. members would be in agreement with what he has said. But I suspect at the same time that if he, on behalf of the government, is allowed to argue the matter procedurally, there is no reason why another 15 members of the House should not be allowed to debate the same matter procedurally.
This is why for some time now I have thought that, in order to keep some control over these questions of privilege, the debate should be limited purely to the statement made by the member who raises a matter by way of question of privilege and a statement by the member who is involved personally in the question raised by way of privilege. This is why I suggested initially that an opportunity should be given to a minister who felt that he has an explanation to give when he thinks such explanation is necessary. I am not suggesting that it was. I am just saying to the minister that we might get ourselves into difficulty, and become involved in a lengthy debate on questions of privilege if, every time a question of privilege were raised, the President of the Privy Council or someone on behalf of the government felt constrained to put forward a procedural argument on the question of privilege and whether there was a prima facie question of privilege. I suggest that it is for the Chair to determine that point. The matter is an important one, but perhaps the minister might like to take my suggestions into consideration and bring his statement to a close.

subtopic: MR. DOUGLAS (NANAIMO-COWICHAN-THE ISLANDS) - STATEMENTS BY MINISTERS RESPECTING MEMORANDUM ON HIRING OF FRANCOPHONES
speechtext:
I thank the President of the Privy Council for his forbearance and again I suggest, with all due respect, that perhaps the practice we have been following has worked rather well. I think hon. members have appeared to want to co-operate with the Chair in following this practice. It seems so much better to consider questions of privilege, to hear the question stated as briefly and lucidly as possible by the hon. member who raises it and not to embark on a procedural argument. I think the practice has functioned rather well until now, and I hope the Chair will continue to have the co-operation of hon. members in following that practice which, I think for the benefit of the House in general, we should follow.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands has given the notice required by section 2 of Standing Order 17 in the following terms:
At two o'clock today I wish to raise a question of privilege arising out of conflicting statements of cabinet ministers which I consider a contempt of Parliament.
Should Your Honour decide that I have a prima facie case of privilege, I am prepared to submit a motion for the consideration of the House.
In a preliminary way, I should mention that since then I have given the matter the most serious thought and consideration. I have looked at precedents and citations and applied my mind as diligently and objectively as possible to the important matter raised by the hon. member. I have also listened with interest to the arguments submitted by the President of the Privy Council and, as I said a moment ago, I do not disagree with any
of the points which he made from a procedural standpoint. I believe he stated correctly what the position is from a procedural point of view of procedure.
I should like to ask in a hypothetical way whether an assertion to the effect that certain proceedings are in contempt of parliament is inherently a matter of privilege as understood by our practice. I have some serious doubts about it. What the hon. member suggests in the notice he has given to the Chair is that being in contempt of parliament constitutes a question of privilege. If all hon. members will look at the definition of privilege which has been cited from time to time in the House and which is reported in May's 17th edition at page 42, they will find that this definition indicates that so-called contempt of parliament does not by itself constitute a question of privilege. It might be an element, of course, it might be part of the general picture, but by itself to say that there has been contempt of parliament and therefore there is a question of privilege is, I suggest to the hon. member, not the complete picture, and that when there is nothing more it does not constitute a question of privilege.
It seems to the Chair that the matter raised by the hon. member may be classified or categorized in one of three ways. First, an hon. member may allege wilful misconduct or wilful intention to mislead the House. As has been pointed out correctly by the President of the Privy Council, there is here a long-established rule which would apply, a rule to which the Chair has alluded from time to time. May I refer hon. members to the ruling of Mr. Speaker Michener, which again the President of the Privy Council quoted. It is reported at page 584 of our Journals for Friday, June 19, 1959:
In my view, simple justice requires that no hon. member should have to submit to investigation of his conduct by the House or a committee until he has been charged with an offence.
I fully recognize that the words uttered by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, as well as the words contained in his notice to the Chair, do not by themselves imply a charge of personal impropriety on the part of the minister. If they did, the hon. member knows as well as I do that by virtue of the long-established practice he would have to make a specific charge in the House and the matter would then be referred almost automatically to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
On the other hand, if the hon. member wishes to press a grievance or to censure a minister or a group of ministers, or the government in general, our practice provides specific procedures to effect such a result. In particular, the hon. member could move a substantive motion, after notice, in the ordinary way. I recognize that this may not be a very helpful suggestion, but it is one of the practices or procedures provided by our Standing Orders. In addition, I suggest that our supply procedures are designed at least in part to achieve such an object.
The third point is that the hon. member's notice is based on the suggestion that conflicting statements have been made by cabinet ministers. In his statement to the House a moment ago the hon. member was suggesting

February 3, 1971

that ministers have made misleading declarations in the course of replying to questions in the House. The Chair has frequently referred to citation 113 in Beauchesne's Fourth Edition which in part states:
But a dispute arising between two members, as to allegations of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege.
On one hand the hon. member contends that there is a conflict in the statements made by one minister and another minister and perhaps statements made by other ministers and an answer given to the House yesterday by the Prime Minister. On the other hand, the President of the Treasury Board argued yesterday that there is no such conflict. Surely this is a matter of debate.
Hon. members may remember that a similar question was raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands on February 26, 1970, as reported at page 4109 of Hansard for that day. The hon. member suggested to the House that there was a conflict between statements on water resources made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The hon. member argued that these allegedly contradictory statements constituted a contempt of parliament and suggested that the matter should be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. After considering all the precedents and our practice, a ruling was made by the Chair concluding that the matter did not constitute a question of privilege.
Again, in this instance, after having considered the precedents and our Standing Orders, I must conclude that there is not a prima facie case of privilege, the only matter which is before the Chair at present, and therefore the motion proposed by the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands cannot be put to the House.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at present a railway can reduce its passenger service over any particular line without making application first to the Canadian Transport Commission. Such application is necessary only when a railway wishes to terminate completely such passenger service. This bill would amend the Railway Act and require an application to the Canadian Transport Commission when a railway wishes to reduce its service. The railway would have to follow the same procedure as when it wishes to terminate a service. This bill is prompted by the action of the CNR in discontinuing service in Northern Ontario and between Montreal and Ottawa.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Part I of Bill C-207 deals with the establishment of a Department of the Environment, and during second reading we had some very interesting debate on this matter. I, myself, made some suggestions to the government but I am quite sure they have received little attention from the minister. Nevertheless, I hope that if I reiterate some points, consideration will be given to them by hon. members and by the departments concerned.
I think that the name "department of the environment" is a misnomer. Everybody would like to see a department of the environment set up. I do not want to be misunderstood on that score, but it seems to me that such a department should be able to deal with all environmental problems all across our nation, and that the environmental aspects of work being done by other departments should come under its scrutiny and control. Unless we
Government Organization Act, 1970 get that type of control in one department, which will co-ordinate our attack on pollution problems, we will not get the job done that should be done.
During the debate on second reading I said that a department of the environment should not be responsible for any specific resource. Once you have a resource department established, its work is primarily directed toward the economic development of that particular resource. If resource development and environmental problems are mixed too closely, there will be major conflict between those in the department who are anxious to see the exploitation of a resource and those who insist that its development be strictly controlled in the interests of the environment.
A real department of the environment should be able to set national standards and co-ordinate enforcement activities. For that reason, I think the government has made a blunder with respect to its proposals in this part of the bill. I repeat that I am not objecting to the establishment of a department of the environment. We should have such a department but it should supervise all the activities of government connected with environmental matters, including fisheries and forestry, water resources and our Arctic areas. To exclude supervision over our Arctic areas from the responsibilities of this department does not make sense.
Only recently we passed an Arctic pollution bill, but responsibility for it is not being transferred to the proposed new department. Our northern territories comprise over 40 per cent of our land mass, but control in this area will still rest with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. A better name for the new department proposed in this bill would be the department of renewable resources. While I am critical of the fact that we are not moving far enough, I must say that in this legislation we have moved further toward pollution control than we have in any other legislation on our statute books.
Canada has an opportunity to take a worldwide lead in dealing with environmental problems. Again, I repeat that we will never adequately solve our pollution problems, or those of the world, until we realize there are three main things linked closely together and which cannot be separated. We may make some progress in some fields, but we will never do a thorough job of pollution control unless we look into these three aspects and their relation to environmental pollution.
One deals with population planning. I am thinking not only in terms of Canada but of the world. We can cut the worldwide pollution rate in half, and yet if the population doubles, there will be as much pollution as there is today, and possibly more. We have to tie our plans to the plans of the United Nations and of other international agencies.
Then, we come to resources. Again, exploitation of resources is linked extremely closely with pollution problems. In the future, I foresee a department of environment coping with this type of resource development and the allocation of our raw materials. One matter which

February 3, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 should be considered by the department of environment is the recycling of materials which we have been using and which we currently have in this nation today. This is where the source of our pollution problems. We are one of the most wasteful nations on the face of this earth. Other nations, such as the nation to the south of us and other industrial nations, face a similar problem.
We dig out minerals in one section of the country, and after they have been through one cycle of use we discard them. Very little effort has been put into recycling. Until we get down to this type of planning and research, we will just be batting our heads against a stone wall so far as adequate pollution control methods are concerned. This is why I stress the absolute need for a department that can overlook the departments concerned and work out a sensible type of approach toward pollution problems.
I will make several suggestions to the government and to the minister. I think that the department of environment should take the responsibility for coordinating and enforcing all current environmental legislation. The way this new department is set up it would not do this. There is nothing in the legislation which provides for the new department enforcing control legislation which we already have on the statute books today. This is why we are in trouble, and why we have stressed this apsect on numerous occasions. It does not make sense to pass laws if they will not be enforced. We have numerous examples of this all over the country.
We would not have a pollution problem in Canada today if we had enforced the regulations which we currently have on the statute books. This lack of enforcement has resulted in the mess we have in the Great Lakes and in the pollution of our navigable rivers. The objective of a department of environment should be to make certain that these regulations are co-ordinated, and that the departments concerned are forced to make sure that companies, individuals, municipalities and others live up to the legislation which is already on our statute books. We have not done this job.
The second point is that any department of environment should be given the task of scrutinizing all activities in the country for their potential environmental impact. I will give you an example. We should have the power we need for this scrutiny under the Navigable Waters Protection Act if, for example, British Columbia decides to build a hydro plant on a river. However, B.C. hydro today is not responsible to any department of government. It does not have to produce a plan to the federal government to show that the building of that hydro plant is a sensible thing.
We should make certain that someone oversees projects of this nature. Some department should be able to say that this project is either beneficial and economic or it is not. It does not make sense to build a dam, thereby flooding hundreds of thousands of acres and doing immense damage to the ecology, without some kind of scrutiny. There is nothing in the statutes today that can stop this type of project from being built with the resultant damage to ecology.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
This is why we are asking for amendments to the bill and for a department which is strong enough to oversee activities of this nature. I will suggest to you that public bodies all over the country, as well as individual citizens, are interested in this type of approach being taken toward such projects. I have just referred to hydro plants. Other types of development could be considered, such as the building of a pipeline down the Mackenzie valley or the drilling for oil up in the north. There must be someone to ensure that our regulations and our basic approach are sound, so that we can leave Canada to future generations in better shape then we found it. But I am afraid that is not going to be so.
There is a third point. I think the department of environment should establish positive reclamation programs for those parts of the country which have already suffered damage. Again, this is an overriding consideration in spite of the narrowness of the bill before us. It does not matter in what part of Canada such damage occurs or in what fields, if damage is being done this department should be able to set up some kind of positive reclamation program and take it to the governments concerned. I am referring to the federal and provincial governments. They should say that this is the type of program needed to reclaim some body of water, some piece of land or some section of air that has been fouled to the point where it is dangerous to the health of Canadians. This bill does not give these powers. Certainly, it is a step forward, but it does not give us the overriding power which we need.
The fourth point I mentioned earlier was that the department should have the power to develop a population policy for this country and to relate it to the resource activities about which I have just spoken.
There are one or two other suggestions which I made the other day which I would like to repeat. I am quite convinced that the government will not set up the type of department which I have outlined. If they will not do that, I suggest the least they can do is to set up an environmental council of Canada similar to the Economic Council of Canada. The environmental council of Canada could be a Crown corporation, but it should be a body that has the power to do a great deal of research. It could act as an adviser to government departments. If there is anything that is desperately needed in Canada, it is a council of this type. It could even work with the over-all department of environment which I suggested should be set up. This is the type of independent body that we need. It should be divorced from the government and should be capable of being extremely critical of government policy, government programs and government direction. I will urge the new minister of the department, once he is appointed, that it be one of the first and main objectives of his department, to get this council rolling. Do not let us wait for six months or six years before setting up this council. We need the advice which such a council can give us.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few comments about the appointment of the minister of the environment consequent on passage of this bill. I will deal with the Problem of pollution. A minister responsible for environmental matters is needed; the task is large. Pollution is one of the major factors in the lives of the people of this country today. Pollution could actually destroy this country. It is probably as lethal as any war or as any intercontinental missile could be. It affects the water, the land, the air; it can involve noise and waste and it is something that parliament has to consider from all angles. In the first instance, pollution is a disease of society and of science. Scientists learned how to control and prevent epidemics, thereby enabling more people to live longer and reproduce. We see the pollution of war, war which has been made possible through the advances of medical science. If science had not advanced, modem war would be impossible. If science had not been able to conquer and then prevent epidemics involving certain diseases, we should not be here arguing about the matter of pollution germ warfare would have looked after that.
The increase in population brought urbanization. As science made further inroads on disease more people were enable to live longer and reproduce. Consequently, the population of the world has grown and will double in the next 30 years. More people have become urbanized. More people moved to the cities and created the problem of pollution. Under sanitary procedures of other days, people poured raw sewage into the rivers and lakes. The rivers and lakes were able to absorb small quantities of raw sewage. But, as city populations grew, the volume of sewage dumped into rivers and lakes also grew. The rivers and lakes could not cope with those large quantities and became more and more contaminated. Today some cities of Canada, particularly on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts as well as those situated on large rivers flowing into the ocean pour raw sewage into the ocean. Cities along the Great Lakes have sewage treatment facilities that are unable to meet the demands made on them so there are overflows of raw sewage. Also, sewage going to the lakes, rivers and streams is finally being deposited in the ocean.
As we know, the people and animals on the earth would be unable to breathe and, hence, unable to live if they could not obtain oxygen. An hon. member said the other day that 70 per cent of our oxygen comes from the ocean. It is produced in the ocean by micro-organisms. The ocean is becoming polluted, and we are discovering that is having an effect on fish such as, for example, swordfish. We were informed in the House that swordfish contain levels of mercury dangerous to human beings eating the fish. Other fish, also, are contaminated with quantities of mercury and are unfit for human consumption. In many cases, these mercury levels may be bringing about mutations and other undetermined problems. We also know that pollution is destroying those organisms
Government Organization Act, 1970
which enable fish to transform the food they feed on into protein. I refer to protein dialysis by plankton. We can see that there is a vicious circle here.
In Canada we have tried to control pollution by introducing legislation such as the Canada Water Act. We have set up authorities under this Act such as the authority in the Northwest Territories which the hon. member who just spoke mentioned, as well as other authorities on the coast under the department of fisheries. Although the Canada Water Act does contain some good provisions, its effectiveness depends largely on cooperation and co-ordination with the provinces. The new minister of the environment must be able to get along with the provinces. There must be communication both ways. The government must be far seeing, and make sure that the old gag we have seen pulled over and over again is not pulled in this area. No one must say, "We will do our share if the other fellow does his share." To be effective, the authority in this matter must be vested in Parliament. I am not saying that provincial rights should be eroded; they should not be. Nevertheless, there must be an indication that we are to move more quickly than in the past and with a better chance of success in this area.
As well as considering the matter of water pollution, we ought to consider the problem of industrial pollution. We have seen factories pouring refuse into our rivers and lakes and polluting them. For instance, the pulp and paper industry and other industries are pouring chemicals and waste products into our lakes and rivers. I sometimes wonder how many industries will be closed down as a result of proceedings taken against them to enforce the law against pollution. What provision is being made to help industries that are financially unable to handle this situation?
In other words, I am asking myself this question, Mr. Chairman, and I think most people here are also asking themselves this question: is it better to ask an industry to move to one of the regional areas and support it with subsidies, even though there is a risk that the industry will not be successful, or is it more businesslike and to the point to keep that industry where it is and assist it to clean up its pollution problem? I do not think this government has grasped that point at all. I think it has run wild all over the land, and particularly in the east. I think its regional incentive program has become an equalization payment program. I think the minister of the new department should consider those points carefully. We are told that there are between 600,000 and 800,000 unemployed; no one knows the exact figures. Could it be that as many as 900,000 are unemployed? The unemployed need our help. They want to work. Extreme caution must be used, and perhaps special treatment given in some cases, to help industry clean up its sewage problem.
We must also consider the people who are paying the 3 per cent surtax which was continued this year. The money these people are paying in taxes is paid out under these incentive programs. I think the provincial and federal governments ought to consider carefully what should be done about an industry that may be polluting.

February 3, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
It may cost little to clean up that pollution. Nevertheless, because of taxation and as a result of sticking to certain guidelines, the profits of such industries may have been so low that they do not have the necessary money with which to clean up the problem. I do not think it is good sense to close an industry merely because it is polluting, thereby causing hundreds of people to become unemployed. There is far too much of this. It does not add up to good common sense to spend ten times the amount of money we would spend on pollution control to establish a new industry in a regional area.
When dealing with the problem of pollution, we must also consider air pollution. Year after year Members of Parliament have seen the air over this city become polluted. Pulp mills and industry across the river in the neighbouring province have been polluting the air. Year after year people have been upset by the fumes they have been breathing, yet Parliament has not done anything about this. I wonder what the new minister of the environment proposes to do about air pollution since air knows no boundaries. This jurisdictional problem relates to the provinces, but also to the United States.
What is going to be done about the problem of air pollution caused by motor vehicles in our large cities? In the United States, as well as in large cities such as Toronto, over 50 per cent of air pollution is due to this cause. This occurs mostly in the rush hours. Pollution forms an umbrella over a city and descends during a rainfall. In addition, pollution causes disease, certain morbidity and a certain amount of sickness. Some authorities have stated that 25 per cent of illness may, partially or wholly, be caused by pollution.
On occasions hundreds of people have lost their lives because of air pollution. Almost 5,000 people in the city of London died in one period of fog. The smog and chemicals irritated the bronchial tubes to the point where these people actually died. These things must be carefully considered, because they are part and parcel of the whole problem. The larger our population becomes, the more pollution we will have. Will the minister of the environment deal with the problems of population control, urbanization, how many people shall live in cities and how many shall live in rural areas? I wonder what the thought of the minister will be on that subject. Something must be done about those problems. It is people who pollute.
I will not deal with all the problems that beset us. I think it proper that we have a minister of the environment. I see the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) in the chamber. I do not want him to get a swelled head because that would be bad. However, his work has been very good; his answers honest and carefully thought out. We must have this type of minister if we are going to do more than just a bit of fancy dressing.
I now want to deal with the question of how this new department will control the problem of pollution. How many committees will be established to deal with the provinces? Population, air and water are interprovincial

and intercountry matters. These problems have not been dealt with as yet. There will be problems with respect to people. Perhaps it will be necessary to relocate them. How will the population of the large cities be controlled? Recently, a bill dealing with abortions was passed by this House. There now seem to be some unsatisfactory aspects of the bill. I am in favour of creating a department of the environment. I believe it is necessary. One cannot be against motherhood or anything that proposes to clean the air, water, and soil.
I now wish to deal with the matter of pollution of Parliament. Included in this bill are matters which will pollute Parliament. I will now dwell on the pollution of Parliament. Departmental ministers are a necessity. We cannot say anything about them in so far as pollution is concerned. The ministers without portfolio are allowed to be foot loose. How many will be appointed? This may be a source of pollution. I have already dealt with the problems of population. I now wish to deal with the proposed increase of ministers without portfolio and ministers of state. The five additional ministers of state will have designated purposes. However, what will the ministers of state without designated purposes do? Are they going to pollute the place with Bureaucracy? Are they going to help the departmental ministers? We would like to have these answers.

Mr. Chairman, clause 3 of Bill C-27 states as follows, and I quote:
There shall be a Department of the Government of Canada called the Department of the Environment-
That covers some ground!
-over which the Minister of the Environment appointed by commission under the Great Seal of Canada shall preside.
Subclause (2) states:
The Minister of the Environment holds office during pleasure and has the management and direction of the Department of the Environment.
That is clear enough. It is an invitation for us to discuss all related matters. A Minister of the Environment is a minister of the environment. I have been rather surprised to see a bill introduced to establish a Department of the Environment.
Government Organization Act, 1970
At a time when all ministers are complaining about a lack of funds to administer their department, the government introduces a bill to set up a new department, that of the Environment. The environment of other ministers, or what? This new department will obviously call for new expenditures! This is a repeat performance of what has been going on for two and a half years with the setting up of commissions and boards: an inquiry board here, a commission there, a commission report, the setting up of a new commission to inquire into the report of the previous commission. We are going from one commission to the other without really knowing where we are heading.
We have established a royal commission on bilingualism at a cost of approximately $15 million to the taxpayer so that we could learn that english is spoken in western Canada and French in the province of Quebec. We did not learn anything else from that commission.
And the Department of the Environment involves new expenditures.
While existing problems go begging for a solution, the government appoints new ministers and new parliamentary secretaries, thereby increasing administrative expenses in the hope of some final solution to Canada's economic problems.
We want to create jobs. However, the more we dwell on the subject, the more the number of unemployed people in Canada increase! And a further increase of their number is forecast within a couple of months, although some slowdown is foreseen thereafter. Meanwhile, the government introduces bills establishing departments.
I earnestly believe that we need no Department of the Environment at the present time, but a national credit office to provide the ministers now in office with the money they require adequately to run their departments.

Mr. Chairman, if I may answer this question, the new department of the environment cannot possibly cover all aspects of the environment. The environment is a very wide subject. The department's main role will be one of co-ordination. There are a number of other departments which in their own way must have an impact on the environment-for example, the Department of Transport in the area of shipping. The Canada Shipping Act deals with a very effective federal power; and the amendments currently being introduced to the Canada Shipping Act, for example, deal very effectively with one aspect of pollution, namely spills from vessels on the high seas, in Canadian territorial waters and fishing zones or indeed in navigable fresh waters in Canada. So, the Department of Transport is clearly involved in the part of the bill dealing with pollution.
Then, there is the Arctic seas pollution bill and the northern inland waters bill. In many ways the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is like a provincial government. It has the equivalent of provincial powers in the north. It must exert powers in respect of rivers, streams and the islands of the north. Legislation pertaining directly to the north is generally administered by that department, as is similar legislation administered by the provinces-that is, the properly instituted provinces of Canada.

Not a day passes that there is not some fresh story about pollution on a large scale. I think most of us are glad to see the present minister is minister-in-waiting of this new department because most of us feel he is very much in earnest and will, to the best of his ability, make a start on tackling this tremendous job, even though there are undoubtedly aspects of the protection of the environment that are not dealt with in this bill. As a result, we may find that other arrangements will have to be made.
The job that confronts us all across Canada is a tremendous one, as we discovered during our study of the Canada Water Act. Indeed, it is becoming increasingly obvious. In the minister's province and mine there is much to be done. For example, starting from the eastern portion of the province, we have the strip mining in British Columbia near the Alberta border which has made the landscape into a moonscape-sterile and terribly ugly. Then, we have the mining and logging problems in the provincial parks. Measures must be taken to protect the forests. In British Columbia, for every seven acres cut only about one acre is reforested, and we know it takes about 75 years to regrow marketable timber on the mountainsides. Then, the Utah Mining Company dumps tailings into the tidewater on the far side of Vancouver Island. And so, on I could go.
I know that the minister will agree that it is not a complete answer to say that provincial jurisdiction is involved here, although we know that that is the case. I really do not believe anyone who thinks about it would feel that we can allow the constitution in its present form to stand in the way of getting at this problem. I think the amendment of the constitution, in its totality, may remain a conversation piece for many years. I remember well the Rowell-Sirois commission back in the 1930's when the amendment of the constitution was considered of tremendous urgency. We are still working on it and it may be a long time before we have a completely new and rational constitution.
I have felt it to be true of other departments of government, and doubly true of the new department of environment, that the minister will have to initiate the
Government Organization Act, 1970 over-all planning in these matters and then go to the provincial governments with propositions that can be discussed and amended, but which will result in action.
He knows very well that in our province, which he and I probably know better than any other province, the people are very anxious to see action in this regard. He also knows that in the province of British Columbia the people are very anxious to be allowed to help. This was very true all across Canada when the matter involved was the cutting down or the removal of phosphates in detergents. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources should be the first one to be thankful that there was such a flood of letters and protests from ordinary people across this country, because it made his job not only easier but perhaps possible within the time he had to accomplish it. The present minister who will handle problems in respect of environment would do well to realize this fact. If ever there was a sector or a field in which the public can help, it is this area of protection of our environment.
Even if we do get things set up, all the policing that can be done through government sources will not be enough. If the minister can arrange things to avail himself of the voluntary policing of the thousands of consumers across this country he will find his job much easier. And that policing will be provided free of charge. People are so concerned about saving our environment that they are willing to report infringements. They are anxious to bring as much pressure to bear as possible^
Ways and means will have to be found within the existing constitutional machinery to provide authority in respect of saving the environment even where there is divided jurisdiction, as is the case in respect of mining, forestry and other aspects of resource conservation. The hon. member for Kootenay West has at least twice made the point that the laws on the statute books are no better than the enforcement of such laws. In years past we have not been sufficiently vigilant and have not realized what is happening to our ecology.
We have now reached the point where we must find new and effective machinery. Instead of waiting until he has a completely new plan in respect of fish, wildlife and other things, the minister should build up the confidence of the public by proceeding on a pilot project. In this way he could win a victory for our environment. In this way he could gain the confidence of the public to a greater extent than through any amount of regulation, talk or negotiation in respect of the larger issues. He could obtain the support to do what he must do.
In British Columbia there is such a pilot project. I have reference to the saving of the Skagit Valley. This morning I was very pleased to find that the Toronto Globe and Mail recognized, in a fair sized editorial article, the value of saving the Skagit Valley in British Columbia. This is the first time I have seen anything of this kind on this scale outside British Columbia.
This editorial recognizes the fact that a valley such as the Skagit River Valley is a great asset, not only to British Columbia but to the whole of Canada. It recognizes that the salavation of this area should be eonsid-

I am sure the minister will not find any objection from the province of British Columbia. I am sure Mr. Bennett would be very glad to be helped out of this difficulty in which he now finds himself. The public is very much aroused about this situation.
This whole matter goes back a long way, in fact further than I want to take it at this time. Back in 1942 the city of Seattle, with the consent of the International Joint Commission, was allowed to flood part of the Skagit Valley behind a dam built within the United States. The city needed more power to support war industries. It also received under this agreement, with the consent of the International Joint Commission, the authority to raise this dam 125 feet higher when necessary, providing the consent of the government of British Columbia was forthcoming.
In 1967 Premier Bennett gave the city of Seattle a 99 year lease for $35,000 a year permitting the flooding of about ten acres of the Skagit River Valley. This is one of the most choice recreation sites anywhere near Vancouver and, indeed, is one of two remaining river valleys suitable for recreational purposes in British Columbia. On the basis of a 99 year lease at $35,000 per year, this works out to about $5.50 per acre.
When Premier Bennett leased this area to the city of Seattle he gave the city something else. He gave a three-year timber cutting permit in order that the Skagit River Valley could be prepared for flooding, a permit now withdrawn under public pressure.
Under the guidance of organizations such as SPEC, which is the equivalent of Pollution Probe in Ontario, the people of Vancouver have realized what is happening. They are beginning to realize that fish spawning grounds there are being destroyed. There will be ten miles of floodded area, but there will be a great deal of spawning area destroyed. They are beginning to realize that mead-owlands on which between 400 and 500 deer are feeding will be destroyed. They realize that a number of species of wildlife will be destroyed because of the flooding of this area. They also realize the tremendous loss of a recreational area within 125 miles of Vancouver which will result fromthis flooding. The people are beginning to fight to save the Skagit River Valley, but they need the help of the minister.

Mr. Chairman, is rising to take part in this discussion, particularly in relation to clause 3 which has to do with measures proposed to establish the new department, I would like to say that the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry, who comes from the same polluted province as I do, will be the new minister of environment in this country, as I understand it.
There are many forms of pollution and environmental impairment, as we all know, but at this time I want to devote the main part of what little I have to say to one aspect of pollution which is rather ignored or down played. I refer to sound pollution. I hope to bring attention to these particular aspects of environmental impairment which exist, particularly in British Columbia. At present we have a threat to our environment in B.C. by air and sea which is posed in the now approved underground nuclear test by the United States in the Aleutian Islands. It has been approved to the extent that money has actually been allocated for this explosion. We all recall what happened a year or two ago in a much smaller test. We can well understand that the public of B.C. will be much exercised at what is now threatened, because a new test in that area will be much larger than the one we have had and survived. It is not impossible that we will experience a tidal wave as a result of this intended blast in the Aleutians. It is taking place in an earthquake prone zone, as we know, and a few years ago when there was an earthquake, B.C. communities such as Port Alberni experienced very high waves and damage as a result.
I want to urge the minister to do whatever he can to get this government to ask the United States to delay or cancel this test until such time as negotiations going on between the United States and the Soviet Union hopefully reach a level of sanity which will end in an agreement to abandon this type of underground nuclear testing. That is one point in connection with the environmental problem facing British Columbians.
Second, I want to urge the minister to do whatever he can to get this government to avert the planned shipment, by U.S. private interests, down the B.C. coast of great quantities of oil from Alaska. These oil shipments are to be carried in tankers which are a threat, as we all know, through spillage of oil to some of the most beautiful areas in coastal Canada. I raised this matter the other day during the question period, and the minister told me that this was a matter which concerned the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Again, I take this opportunity to urge him to do what he can to get the Secretary of State for External Affairs to step up activities to avert this very threatening pollution problem.
Third, I want to allude briefly to a problem which affects a number of British Columbians. We have about two million people in B.C. over half of whom within a very few miles on half of one per cent of the land area. A good many of them live in and around my constituency. These people are faced with another threat of pollution in the form of coal cars, trains carrying coal coming up from the United States through the White Rock Crescent Beach and Ocean Park shipment points. These are among the best recreational and residential waterfront areas. I urge the minister, when established in his new post, to take whatever measures he can think of to alleviate the situation.
Having said that, I would like to speak now about a form of pollution about which I am particularly concerned. I have placed on the order paper a bill on the subject of noise or sound pollution. Before I do that, however, I wish the minister every good fortune in whatever endeavours he undertakes in his capacity as minister of environment. I know he means well in every case where he shows his intention, and he will certainly have the support not only of his party but of the people of British Columbia.
The fourth form of pollution beyond that of air, land and sea, is noise or sound pollution. In my view, this type of pollution should be under study by a standing committee of the House which concerns itself with all matters of pollution. The time is overdue when sound pollution should be recognized as a health danger to individuals and communities. In urging that this form of pollution be recognized as part of the environmental problem with which this legislation sets out to deal, I want to quote very briefly from a few articles which have been published on the subject. I will quote now from a report in the Ottawa Citizen of a Boston meeting which reads in part as follows:
Slowly, in a sneaky sort of way, noise is ruining the health of hundreds of thousands of North Americans and bringing death years closer for thousands.
That's the message which has been preached over and over again in the first few days of a session on noise pollution at the annual meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science here
There's not much in the frightening medical evidence that is brand new, but it's the first time that it has ever been put together like this, in a discussion drawing scientists from Canada, Australia, Germany, Argentina and the U.S.S.R....
-noise isn't good for .. . just about every bodily function you can name and that doesn't count hearing because the scientists aren't even talking about that problem since it has been well publicized.
Noise isn't good for you,. .. because it causes the small blood human body shows little inclination to adapt to repeated noises like the sound of horns blowing outside the window at night.
Noise isn't good for you, . . .because it causes the small blood vessels in the body to contract and then expand involuntarily. This contraction happens even to people who are deaf and eventually the weakening of elasticity in the blood vessels because of it leads to circulatory problems and could be a contributing factor in strokes and heart attacks.
The article goes on to list the reports of other scientists concerning the seriousness of noise pollution.

May I quote from another editorial in the Globe and Mail. It reads
A two day symposium on noise pollution conducted by the American Medical Association ... estimated that environmental din is doubling in intensity every decade. Even bigger jumps are in prospect with the mounting volume of air traffic-expected to triple by 1975-and the advent of supersonic transport planes with their sonicboom capacity to shatter eardrums as well as window panes.
But planes are only a fraction of the cacophony. Heavy traffic clocks in at around 80 decibels or just about the tolerable level. A motorcycle can shoot that up to 110 decibels, a siren to 125 decibels (one doctor complained recently that ambulance sirens were killing more patients than they were saving) ...
There is a great deal of literature on this subject, which I hope the new minister of the environment will read. I hope, as a result, that the government will act.
Last March I was glad to receive assurances from three ministries that action to deal with the matter of sound pollution is to be taken. The Minister of Labour replied to a letter I had sent him and said that regulations pertaining to noise control and hearing conservation in industries subject to federal jurisdiction and in the Public Service of Canada are being developed pursuant to the Canada Labour (Safety) Code. Another reply from the Minister of National Health and Welfare said that the department intends to increase its activities in these areas. Finally, I received a letter from the President of the Treasury Board. It said that sound and man's sensitivity to it are being studied under ten general headings.
I received these assurances last March, almost one year ago. I hope that such action as was indicated in those replies has been taken by the departments concerned. In any event I intend to keep on making representations, either at the committee level or at any other level, for the minister to include sound pollution in the protection of the environment.

The answer, Mr. Chairman, is yes. I mentioned that there were a number of other departments which are vitally concerned about the environment, departments such as the Department of National Health and Welfare. Clean air is essential to health and the Department of National Health and Welfare will continue to be concerned about the quality of the air around us. The environmental health unit of the Department of National Health and Welfare has been transferred already and will be part of the new department of the environment. Nevertheless, remaining within the department of health will be others who are concerned about the health of human beings in industry, the health of people as distinct from the general well-being of the environment. The new department of the environment
Government Organization Act, 1970 will therefore be working closely with the Department of National Health and Welfare. The people who have been transferred from the occupational health unit to the department of the environment will, themselves, be working closely with the medical people of the department.
I might mention other departments. Clearly, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is concerned about fuels and the quality of fuels. Clearly, the sulphur content of a fuel has a great deal to do with the quality of the effluent being discharged. The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources will be concerned about such things as industries that use sulphur bearing coal and will be vitally interested, far into the future, in that aspect of the pollution problem. Clearly, the people in the department of the environment will be working closely with the people in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Reference has been made to transportation, and to aircraft. Aeronautics as well as shipping will be a matter for the Parliament of Canada. The Department of Transport focusses particularly on this kind of transportation. It can regulate the devices used by aircraft, the design of ships, and so on. Personnel in the Department of Transport will be working closely with the meteorological service, which is being transferred to the new department of the environment. The meteorological service looks at the weather side of things; weather forecasting is essential to transportation. So, there must be co-operation, again, between the "met" service, the new department of the environment and the Department of Transport. Among those three departments, transport, energy, mines and resources and national health and welfare, there will be close liaison in future with the department of the environment.

I cannot answer the hon. member's question in precise numbers. He referred to the fact that an earlier piece of legislation was repealed when the Canada Water Act was introduced. Under the former legislation, the federal government, provincial governments and local municipalities or authorities carried out certain river development projects, usually on a modest scale. They varied in size from province to province. Under the original act, the federal government paid 37.5 per cent, the provincial government 37.5 per cent and the local body 25 per cent.
The Canada Water Act which superseded the previous legislation is much more comprehensive. It envisages many kinds of river development such as whole river basins or single tributaries. It covers any conceivable water development in which there is a need for several levels of government, including the federal government, to participate. The basic philosophy is that each level of government should make a contribution which reflects its constitutional responsibilities. If there is a major concern with navigation on a river or stream, there is a federal involvement. If there is a hydro requirement or capability there is probably just a provincial involvement. If fisheries are involved, particularly on the ocean coasts, there is a federal fisheries involvement. If there is a flood control aspect, more than likely there is a provincial involvement. If a development is entirely for hydro, it would be 100 per cent provincial. If a project involves hydro, navigation, flood control and fisheries, the contribution will vary depending on the benefits.
If the benefits of a project are mostly in the federal area, it will probably be largely financed as a federally supported development. If the benefits are largely provincial or local, the financing will fall that way. The expect-

ed benefits will be the determining factor of shares of cost rather than the precise formula laid down in the earlier legislation. Because there is not a precise formula, I do not want the hon. member to think that there is not a way of getting around this problem. It can be argued that double this figure is reasonable, but Sweden has not taken this view. A conference is to be held in Ottawa in February to which experts are coming from all parts of the world. We are focussing on this problem and hopefully we shall be able to provide more information which will help us to set standards which are realistic in the light of that new information. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my answer would be this: We can have national standards, we must have national standards and we will have national standards. The hon. member asks how. We can develop national standards-I am talking more in legal or constitutional terms here- for industries under federal jurisdiction, and some of these are very large. Any industry that has an impact upon our fisheries in so far as its water effluent is concerned can be required to meet the standards under the federal Fisheries Act, because these standards are national in scope and in impact.
There are other industries that come totally within provincial jurisdiction. In many water situations, to regulate properly a body of water you must regulate not just provincial development of water but federal development as well, and in such a case a joint body may be appropriate. If so, we could proceed, for example, under the Canada Water Act or under a similar provision for federal-provincial co-operation under the terms of a clean air act.
In all these instances we would insist that the national standard that we had developed would be the standard to be employed in the joint development in that particular area, so that through federal and provincial agreement it would be possible to bring about the enforcement of national standards. You do not do this through direct federal legislation without reference to the province concerned. In that case you would have to have an agreement with the province relative to the particular industry in that province.
Government Organization Act, 1970
There is a third way to bring about national standards, and this is what we are really doing at the moment with the pulp and paper industry. We are working closely with the provinces and the pulp and paper industry, along with experts from several other countries, in the development of standards that we believe the provincial pollution control boards will adopt as well as our own authorities. Through thorough discussion and sweet reason we believe we will arrive at standards which will in fact be national standards that are applied by the provinces because they believe in them, not because there is federal jurisdiction in every instance within the provinces. So through co-operation and certainly careful discussions we can set standards. The hon. member asks if there are difficulties. The biggest single difficulty is that relating to older plants. We can readily develop standards that apply to new plants by requiring that new plants henceforth must be designed to produce effluent of a quality stipulated in the regulations.
Those regulations and standards have to be the objectives toward which the old plants must progressively be upgraded. The unkown element in this is, how long will it take for the old plants to come up to that standard? In an industry that is totally within a province and totally within provincial jurisdiction, the matter must be left primarily with the province to negotiate with the firm in order to bring this about. There is just no way in which the federal law can reach directly into that situation or do anything about it.
Admittedly, if there is a fisheries aspect or a navigable waters aspect or a flood control aspect and so on, Ottawa can get into it. I am referring to situations where there are no federal aspects, legislation or federal laws that apply. These are the difficult areas.

If it does not conform with our national standards it will be out. The standard can be higher but it certainly cannot be lower than the standards we set for that industry. Wherever we invest federal money, wherever we have federal power and wherever we have agreement with a province for joint management agencies, the federal standards will obtain. In this regard, we will have national standards.
However, we do have two levels of government in this country and sometimes there may be little pockets where there is no federal jurisdiction or avenue for federal participation. It is conceivable there would be different standards under those circumstances, although I do not expect to see much of that. There will be none of it in so far as my department is concerned. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think we are faced with some of the same problems that we might be faced with if we had different standards from province to province. If we have different standards from nation to nation, we will have difficulties, particularly trans-border difficulties. However, with respect to pollutants that are moving around the earth and are universal in their effect, I think we will quickly see international agreements as to standards. There will be many standards that will be worldwide in their effect. There will be considerable pressures develop, especially from nations which are cleaning up, on nations which are not cleaning up as rapidly as they are doing.
I was recently at a conference in Washington. The concern expressed there was that the nations that were cleaning up rapidly might set up barriers of one kind or another against nations that were not cleaning up their industry. In other words-don't buy dirty products. Already, a tendency is developing for standards to be applied internationally, as well as inter-provincially, or nationally within Canada.
There is some value in being first. There is some value in cleaning up first. In British Columbia, where a lot of pulp mills are new, those on freshwater salmon rivers have been cleaning up. In fact they were forced to clean up, but the clean up technology had more or less to be developed from scratch. Engineering consultant services in this field came into being, and several of these firm are being retained by Sweden and Russia to show them how to clean up their industries. By being first we can get our toe in the door with new technology, which can provide new opportunities for trade as well.
But Finland does not want to clean up its pulp mills unless its competitors do the same. However, with Canada cleaning up its mills, and Sweden doing likewise Finland will be forced to take similar steps. There is a movement in this direction, and there is a great deal of public opinion behind it, not only in Canada but worldwide. So, I think we will see standards develop internationally as well as in Canada. There will be a tendency toward uniformity of standards and to the avoidance of pollution havens.

When the answer is found to the cleaning up of its effluents it is an answer-and this includes standards-which can be applied across the country to all new kraft mills, and progressively to older ones as time and money opportunities present themselves to make the changes.

In other words these are particular situations rather than a single industry to which a single cleaning up procedure would readily apply. We intend to tackle the job, but it is a bigger and much more complicated one than the pulp and paper industry.
